subject: science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The concept of a pure substance
Diffusion in terms of the particle model
Simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography

questions.lo: The concept of a pure substance
questions.q: In science, what is a pure substance?
options: A natural material with nothing added to it
A material that looks clear and clean
Just one substance, with nothing mixed in
A single element, but not a compound
questions.explain: Yes. A pure substance is a single element or a single compound with nothing else in it, such as distilled water or copper.
optionWhy: You may have thought 'pure' means natural, as on food labels. In fact a natural material such as spring water or rock salt usually contains several substances, so it is not pure.
You may have thought you can see whether something is pure. In fact salty water looks clear and clean but is a mixture of two substances.
Yes. A pure substance is a single element or a single compound with nothing else in it, such as distilled water or copper.
You may have thought a compound cannot be pure because it has two elements. In fact pure water, H₂O, is one substance, a compound, so it is pure.

questions.lo: The concept of a pure substance
questions.q: A label says 'Pure spring water: natural, with nothing added'. Spring water has minerals dissolved in it. What is it to a scientist?
options: A mixture of water and minerals
A pure substance, as it is natural
A pure substance, as it looks so clear
A compound of water and minerals
questions.explain: Yes. It contains water and dissolved minerals, which are not joined, so it is a mixture. To a scientist it is not pure.
optionWhy: Yes. It contains water and dissolved minerals, which are not joined, so it is a mixture. To a scientist it is not pure.
You may have thought 'pure' means natural or with nothing added. In fact, in science, pure means one substance only, and spring water contains several.
You may have thought a clear liquid must be pure. In fact dissolved minerals cannot be seen, so the water looks clear but is a mixture.
You may have thought the minerals join with the water when they dissolve. In fact dissolving does not make a compound: the minerals are mixed in, not joined, so it is a mixture.

questions.lo: The concept of a pure substance
questions.q: The diagram shows the particles in a sample of gas. Which statement about the sample is correct?
options: It is pure, as it has only elements
It is a mixture of two elements
It is one compound of X and Y
It is pure, as it is all one gas
questions.explain: Yes. There are two kinds of particle: pairs of X atoms (element X) and pairs of Y atoms (element Y). They are not joined to each other, so the sample is a mixture, not a pure substance.
optionWhy: You may have thought a sample made only of elements is one element. In fact it has two different kinds of particle, X₂ and Y₂, so it is two substances mixed.
Yes. There are two kinds of particle: pairs of X atoms (element X) and pairs of Y atoms (element Y). They are not joined to each other, so the sample is a mixture, not a pure substance.
You may have thought any sample with two kinds of atom is a compound. In fact no X atom is joined to a Y atom, so no compound is present.
You may have thought a sample that is all gas, and looks the same throughout, is one substance. In fact it contains two different kinds of particle, so it is a mixture.

questions.lo: The concept of a pure substance
questions.q: Rock salt is dug from the ground. Salt is extracted from it by dissolving, filtering and evaporating. Which is purer, and why?
options: The rock salt, as it is natural and untouched
The rock salt, as extracting is a chemical change
Both are equally pure, as both are just salt
The extracted salt, as the rock and soil are removed
questions.explain: Yes. Dissolving and filtering leave the insoluble rock and soil behind, so the extracted salt contains far fewer other substances. It is the same salt, just separated from the rest.
optionWhy: You may have thought natural means pure. In fact rock salt is salt mixed with rock and soil, so it is a mixture and less pure.
You may have thought dissolving, filtering and evaporating are chemical changes that turn the salt into something new. In fact they are physical processes: they only separate the salt from the rock.
You may have thought anything called 'salt' is one substance. In fact rock salt also contains rock and soil, so it is less pure than the extracted salt.
Yes. Dissolving and filtering leave the insoluble rock and soil behind, so the extracted salt contains far fewer other substances. It is the same salt, just separated from the rest.

questions.lo: Mixtures, including dissolving
questions.q: Sugar is added to water and dissolves. This makes a sugar solution. Which is the solute?
options: The water it dissolves in
The sugar solution as a whole
The sugar that dissolves
Nothing, as the sugar has gone
questions.explain: Yes. The solute is the substance that dissolves, here the sugar. The water is the solvent, and the sugar solution is the mixture made.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up solute and solvent. In fact the liquid the sugar dissolves in, the water, is the solvent; the solute is the sugar.
You may have mixed up 'solute' and 'solution', which sound alike. In fact the solution is the whole mixture; the solute is only the sugar that dissolves.
Yes. The solute is the substance that dissolves, here the sugar. The water is the solvent, and the sugar solution is the mixture made.
You may have thought the sugar disappears when it dissolves. In fact it is still there, spread out as particles too small to see, so the sugar is the solute.

questions.lo: Mixtures, including dissolving
questions.q: Sugar is stirred into hot tea until it can no longer be seen. What has happened to the sugar?
options: It has melted and become liquid sugar
It has gone and is no longer in the tea
It reacted with water to make a new compound
Its particles have spread out in the water
questions.explain: Yes. The sugar has dissolved: its particles have spread out among the water particles. The sugar is still there, which is why the tea tastes sweet.
optionWhy: You may have thought dissolving and melting are the same. In fact the tea is far too cool to melt sugar; the sugar has dissolved, not melted.
You may have thought sugar you cannot see has disappeared. In fact it is still in the tea, spread out as tiny particles, and its mass is still there.
You may have thought dissolving is a chemical reaction. In fact no new substance is made: the sugar could be got back by evaporating the water.
Yes. The sugar has dissolved: its particles have spread out among the water particles. The sugar is still there, which is why the tea tastes sweet.

questions.lo: Mixtures, including dissolving
questions.q: Chalk powder is stirred into water. The water turns cloudy, and later the chalk settles at the bottom. What does this show?
options: Chalk does not dissolve in water
Chalk has dissolved to make a solution
Chalk dissolves with more stirring
Chalk reacts to make a new substance
questions.explain: Yes. Chalk is insoluble in water: its bits make the water cloudy and then settle out. A solution would be see-through, and nothing would settle out.
optionWhy: Yes. Chalk is insoluble in water: its bits make the water cloudy and then settle out. A solution would be see-through, and nothing would settle out.
You may have thought the cloudy water is a solution. In fact a solution is see-through and nothing settles out; the chalk bits settle because the chalk has not dissolved.
You may have thought stirring for longer would make it dissolve. In fact stirring only speeds up dissolving; chalk is insoluble, so stirring cannot make it dissolve.
You may have thought the chalk dissolves and that dissolving is a reaction. In fact no new substance is made: the chalk is only mixed with the water and settles out again.

questions.lo: Mixtures, including dissolving
questions.q: Salt is dissolved in water in a sealed flask. How does the mass of the solution compare with the mass of the salt and water before?
options: Less, as the salt has disappeared
Less, as dissolved salt weighs nothing
The same, as the salt is still there
More, as salty water is denser
questions.explain: Yes. The salt particles are still there, spread out among the water particles, and the flask is sealed, so nothing escapes. Mass of solution = mass of salt + mass of water.
optionWhy: You may have thought the salt is gone because you cannot see it. In fact its particles are still in the water, so its mass still counts.
You may have thought dissolved salt floats and so weighs nothing. In fact every salt particle keeps its mass, wherever it is in the water.
Yes. The salt particles are still there, spread out among the water particles, and the flask is sealed, so nothing escapes. Mass of solution = mass of salt + mass of water.
You may have thought a denser liquid must have more mass. In fact salty water is denser, but its mass is only the salt plus the water: nothing extra is added.

questions.lo: Diffusion in terms of the particle model
questions.q: In the particle model, what causes diffusion?
options: Particles that want to spread out
A push from wind or stirring
Particles reacting with each other
Particles moving about at random
questions.explain: Yes. Particles in liquids and gases move about all the time in all directions. This random movement makes them spread out and mix, with nothing pushing them.
optionWhy: You may have thought particles spread because they want to. In fact particles have no wants: their random movement mixes them.
You may have thought something must push the particles. In fact diffusion happens even in perfectly still air or water; wind and stirring just speed up mixing.
You may have thought the particles react when they mix. In fact diffusion is a physical process: the particles mix without joining, and no new substance is made.
Yes. Particles in liquids and gases move about all the time in all directions. This random movement makes them spread out and mix, with nothing pushing them.

questions.lo: Diffusion in terms of the particle model
questions.q: In the particle model, why is diffusion faster at a higher temperature?
options: The particles move about faster
The particles all get a bit bigger
The heat pushes the particles along
The particles want to spread out more
questions.explain: Yes. At a higher temperature the particles move faster, so they spread out and mix more quickly.
optionWhy: Yes. At a higher temperature the particles move faster, so they spread out and mix more quickly.
You may have thought particles grow when they are heated. In fact particles stay the same size; they move faster, which is why diffusion speeds up.
You may have thought heat pushes the particles. In fact heat is not a push: heating makes each particle move faster by itself.
You may have thought hot particles are more eager to spread. In fact particles have no wants; they simply move faster at a higher temperature.

questions.lo: Diffusion in terms of the particle model
questions.q: The diagram shows gas X diffusing through gas Y in a closed box. Which statement about the X particles is correct?
options: Every X particle moves only to the right
They move right because they want more room
They move only when the closed box is shaken
Each moves at random, but overall more go right
questions.explain: Yes. Every particle moves at random in all directions. There are more X particles on the left, so more of them happen to move right than left: the net movement is from higher to lower concentration.
optionWhy: You may have thought each particle follows the rule 'high to low concentration'. In fact each particle moves at random; the rule only describes the overall result.
You may have thought the particles are looking for space. In fact particles have no wants; random movement is enough to spread them out.
You may have thought diffusion needs a push. In fact gas particles move all the time on their own, so X spreads through the still box without shaking.
Yes. Every particle moves at random in all directions. There are more X particles on the left, so more of them happen to move right than left: the net movement is from higher to lower concentration.

questions.lo: Diffusion in terms of the particle model
questions.q: A drop of ink is put into a beaker of still water. A day later, the colour is even all through the water. What are the ink particles doing now?
options: They have stopped, as they are spread out
They have joined water in a new compound
They are still moving in all directions
They are still looking for more room
questions.explain: Yes. In a liquid the particles never stop moving: they move about at random in all directions. The colour stays even because, on average, as many ink particles move one way as the other.
optionWhy: You may have thought diffusion ends with the particles still. In fact the particles keep moving; the colour stays even because equal numbers move each way.
You may have thought the ink reacts with the water as it spreads. In fact diffusion is a physical process: the ink particles only mix with the water particles.
Yes. In a liquid the particles never stop moving: they move about at random in all directions. The colour stays even because, on average, as many ink particles move one way as the other.
You may have thought particles move because they want more room. In fact particles have no wants: they keep moving in all directions, even once the colour is the same all through.

questions.lo: Simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
questions.q: You want to get back both the water and the salt from salty water. Which method should you use?
options: Separate it by distillation
Separate it by evaporation
Separate it by filtration
Separate it by chromatography
questions.explain: Yes. Distillation boils off the water and cools the vapour in a condenser to collect it as pure water, while the salt stays behind in the flask.
optionWhy: Yes. Distillation boils off the water and cools the vapour in a condenser to collect it as pure water, while the salt stays behind in the flask.
You may have thought evaporation collects the water. In fact in evaporation the water vapour escapes into the air, so only the salt is kept.
You may have thought filter paper can trap dissolved salt. In fact the dissolved salt passes through the paper with the water, so nothing is separated.
You may have thought chromatography can separate any mixture. In fact it shows which dyes are in a mixture; it cannot give you back the water and the salt.

questions.lo: Simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
questions.q: Salty water is poured through filter paper in a funnel. What comes through the paper?
options: Water, with the salt melted in it
Water, with the salt dissolved in it
Only water, as the paper traps the salt
Only water, as the salt has vanished away
questions.explain: Yes. The dissolved salt is spread out as particles far smaller than the holes in the paper, so it passes through with the water. Nothing is separated.
optionWhy: You may have thought the salt has melted. In fact it has dissolved; salt melts only at a very high temperature. The dissolved salt does pass through the paper.
Yes. The dissolved salt is spread out as particles far smaller than the holes in the paper, so it passes through with the water. Nothing is separated.
You may have thought filter paper can trap dissolved salt. In fact only undissolved bits are trapped; dissolved salt passes through with the water.
You may have thought dissolved salt has disappeared. In fact it is still there, spread out in the water, and it passes through the paper with the water.

questions.lo: Simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
questions.q: The diagram shows a paper chromatogram of a black ink. What does it show about the ink?
options: It is one dye that has split into new dyes
It is one substance, since it looks black
It is a mixture of more than one dye
The top spot has the smallest particles
questions.explain: Yes. Each spot is a different dye that was carried a different distance by the solvent. Three spots means the black ink contains at least three dyes.
optionWhy: You may have thought chromatography makes new substances. In fact it is a physical separation: the three dyes were already in the ink.
You may have thought a single colour means a single substance. In fact the ink looks black because several dyes are mixed, as the three spots show.
Yes. Each spot is a different dye that was carried a different distance by the solvent. Three spots means the black ink contains at least three dyes.

You may have thought the paper sorts particles by size, like a sieve, so the smallest go furthest. In fact each dye is carried a different distance because of how well it dissolves in the solvent and sticks to the paper, not because of its size.

questions.lo: Simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
questions.q: A mixture contains sand, salt and water. Which plan gives dry salt with no sand in it?
options: Filter, then evaporate the liquid that comes through
Evaporate first, then filter the dry solid that is left
Filter, then scrape the salt off the filter paper
Distil, then collect the salt that drips out
questions.explain: Yes. Filtering traps the insoluble sand while the dissolved salt passes through with the water. Evaporating that filtrate then leaves the salt as dry crystals.
optionWhy: Yes. Filtering traps the insoluble sand while the dissolved salt passes through with the water. Evaporating that filtrate then leaves the salt as dry crystals.
You may have thought the order does not matter. In fact evaporating first leaves salt and sand mixed as one dry solid, and filtering a dry solid separates nothing.
You may have thought filter paper traps the dissolved salt. In fact only the sand stays on the paper; the salt passes through with the water.
You may have thought the salt boils off with the water. In fact salt has a far higher boiling point, so pure water drips out and the salt and sand stay in the flask.

questions.lo: The identification of pure substances
questions.q: How does a pure solid melt?
options: Over a range of temperatures
At 0 °C, just as ice does
Only at a very hot temperature
At exactly one temperature
questions.explain: Yes. A pure solid melts at one sharp, fixed temperature, its melting point. The temperature stays the same until it has all melted.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up the two tests. In fact it is a mixture that melts over a range; a pure solid melts at one fixed temperature.
You may have thought every pure solid melts at 0 °C, like ice. In fact 0 °C is water's melting point; other pure substances have their own.
You may have thought melting always needs a high temperature. In fact melting points can be low or high: ice melts at 0 °C. What matters is that a pure solid melts at one fixed temperature.
Yes. A pure solid melts at one sharp, fixed temperature, its melting point. The temperature stays the same until it has all melted.

questions.lo: The identification of pure substances
questions.q: The graph shows the temperature of two solids, P and Q, as each is heated and melts. Which statement is correct?
options: Q melts over a wide range, so Q is pure
P melts at one fixed temperature, so P is pure
Both are solids, so both are pure substances
Neither melts at 0 °C, so neither is pure
questions.explain: Yes. P's temperature stays flat while it melts, so it melts at one fixed temperature: it is pure. Q's temperature keeps rising as it melts, so it melts over a range: it is a mixture.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up the two tests. In fact melting over a range, as Q does, shows a mixture; a flat part at one fixed temperature, as P shows, means pure.
Yes. P's temperature stays flat while it melts, so it melts at one fixed temperature: it is pure. Q's temperature keeps rising as it melts, so it melts over a range: it is a mixture.
You may have thought any solid material is one substance. In fact a solid can be a mixture; a mixture melts over a range of temperatures, as Q does.
You may have thought pure substances must melt at 0 °C, like ice. In fact each pure substance has its own melting point; P's flat part shows it is pure.

questions.lo: The identification of pure substances
questions.q: Two inks are tested by paper chromatography. Ink S gives one spot. Ink T gives three spots. Which conclusion is correct?
options: S is a mixture, and T may be pure
Both are pure, since each is one ink
T's dyes were made by the test
S may be pure; T is a mixture
questions.explain: Yes. A pure substance gives only one spot, so S may be pure (more tests would check). T separates into three spots, so it contains at least three dyes: it is a mixture.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up the two results. In fact one spot is what a pure substance gives; several spots show a mixture of dyes.
You may have thought anything called one ink is one substance. In fact an ink can be a mixture of dyes, as the three spots from T show.
You may have thought chromatography makes new substances. In fact it only separates the dyes that were already in T, so T is a mixture.
Yes. A pure substance gives only one spot, so S may be pure (more tests would check). T separates into three spots, so it contains at least three dyes: it is a mixture.

questions.lo: The identification of pure substances
questions.q: Pure water boils at 100 °C. How does salty water boil?
options: Lower than 100 °C, over a range
Higher than 100 °C, over a range
At exactly 100 °C, like water
At one fixed temperature above 100 °C
questions.explain: Yes. Salty water is a mixture, so it boils over a range of temperatures, starting above 100 °C and rising as the water boils away.
optionWhy: You may have thought impurities always lower the boiling point. In fact dissolved salt makes water boil above 100 °C.
Yes. Salty water is a mixture, so it boils over a range of temperatures, starting above 100 °C and rising as the water boils away.
You may have thought dissolved salt does not change the boiling point. In fact the salt makes the water boil above 100 °C, and over a range.
You may have thought a mixture boils at one fixed temperature. In fact it is a pure substance that boils at a fixed temperature; salty water boils over a range.

specSource: National Curriculum in England: science programme of study, Key Stage 3; Chemistry — Pure and impure substances
